title: Context clues, synonyms and antonyms
blurb: Work out an unfamiliar word from the one sentence around it, pick synonyms and antonyms in the right sense, and choose the meaning a multiple-meaning word has in context.
question: “Unlike his garrulous roommate, who could talk for hours about anything, Mateo rarely spoke at meals.” You have never seen the word “garrulous.” How can the sentence itself tell you what it means, and how do you avoid the trap answer?

teach.body: Context clues are the hints in the words around an unfamiliar word that reveal its meaning. A HESI A2 vocabulary item gives one sentence of about 8 to 25 words, then asks for the best definition, a synonym or an opposite. Plain English: cover the word, read the rest of the sentence, and let it tell you what belongs in the gap. The same skill decides which meaning a word with several senses has.

head: Clue type
Signal words
One-sentence example
rows: or, that is, in other words
octogenarians, in other words, in their 80s
precarious, so he held the ladder
teach.caption: Real HESI items do not define the word for you; the clue narrows it, and you finish the job.

teach.h: Let the signal word choose the clue

root.label: Find the signal near the word

teach.caption: No signal word? Use the general sense of the whole sentence.

teach.body: Priya, a nursing applicant, practices on four sentences. “Unlike sedentary patients, early walkers build strength faster”: contrast, so sedentary means inactive. “The floor was slick, so walking there was precarious”: cause and effect, so precarious means unsafe. “Aids such as walkers and canes are on every floor”: example, so aids are helpful devices. “The bruise was tender when pressed”: the touch decides the sense, sore, not loving.

steps.label: Cover the word
steps.sub: do not guess from its look

steps.label: Substitute
steps.sub: try each option in the gap

steps.label: Check
steps.sub: same meaning, sense and part of speech

teach.caption: If an option makes the sentence contradict its own clue, it is wrong, however good it sounds.

rows.label: Must match
values: the sense used and part of speech
the sense used and part of speech

teach.caption: Degree matters: copious is not 'some,' and negligible is not 'none.'

head: Trap
What it looks like
rows: Fits the sentence's subject, not the word
A real meaning the sentence rules out
Meaning of a similar word: eminent vs imminent
The trait of the person being contrasted
Same meaning offered when the opposite is asked
teach.caption: Trap answers are often real meanings of real words. That is why substitution, not familiarity, decides.

teach.text: In a contrast clue the meaning is the OPPOSITE of the nearby description. In “Unlike his garrulous roommate, Mateo rarely spoke,” the word “quiet” describes Mateo, not the roommate. The HESI A2 loves to offer “quiet” as a choice. Garrulous means talkative.

items: Six clue types: definition, synonym, antonym/contrast, example, cause and effect, general sense.
Predict your own word first, then substitute each option.
Synonyms and antonyms must match the sense used and the part of speech.
Multiple-meaning words: the rest of the sentence picks the sense.
Traps: topic fit, other sense, look-alikes, contrast flips, synonym-for-antonym.

summary: You can now decode an unfamiliar word from a single sentence using definition, synonym, contrast, example, cause-and-effect and general-sense clues. You can also choose synonyms and antonyms in the right sense and pick the meaning a multiple-meaning word has in its sentence.

A.q: Unlike her outgoing sister, the reticent patient rarely shared her worries with the care team. Based on the context, what does reticent mean?
A.why: “Unlike” contrasts her with an outgoing sister, and she rarely shares her worries. Reticent means reserved.

whyNot.0: Outgoing describes the sister, the other side of the contrast: the contrast-flip trap.
whyNot.1: Not sharing worries is a choice, not forgetting; the contrast is about how open she is.
whyNot.3: Nothing in the sentence describes irritation or hurry.

A.q: Pack basic toiletries, such as a toothbrush, soap and shampoo, for the overnight hospital stay. Based on the context, what are toiletries?
A.why: “Such as” introduces examples; a toothbrush, soap and shampoo are all items for washing and grooming.

whyNot.0: Snacks are also packed for a stay, a topic fit, but none of the examples is food.
whyNot.2: Medications are a topic fit for a hospital, but the examples are for washing.
whyNot.3: Clothes are packed for an overnight stay, but none of the examples is clothing.

A.q: Because the ladder was precarious on the wet floor, the janitor waited for a coworker to hold it. Based on the context, what does precarious mean?
A.why: Cause and effect: the ladder needed someone to hold it on a wet floor, so it was unsteady and unsafe.

whyNot.0: A heavy ladder would not need holding because of a wet floor; the clue is about stability.
whyNot.1: Being new says nothing about the danger the wet floor creates.
whyNot.3: A folded ladder could not be climbed, so no one would need to hold it.

B.q: To save money for nursing school, Malik became frugal and cooked every meal at home. Which word is closest in meaning to frugal as used in this sentence?
B.why: Saving money and cooking at home point to careful spending. Frugal means thrifty.

whyNot.0: Wasteful is the opposite of frugal.
whyNot.2: Cooking every meal is a topic fit for hunger, but frugal is about spending.
whyNot.3: Home cooking can be healthy, but the sentence's purpose is saving money.

B.q: The once vibrant garden behind the clinic looked drab after weeks without rain. Which word means the opposite of drab as used in this sentence?
B.why: Drab means dull and lacking color, so its opposite is colorful (like the once vibrant garden).

whyNot.0: Dull is a synonym of drab, not its opposite: the synonym-for-antonym trap.
whyNot.1: Dry is a topic fit (no rain) but is not the opposite of drab.
whyNot.3: Overgrown describes growth, not color; it is unrelated rather than opposite.

B.q: Her labor lasted fourteen hours before the baby was born early Tuesday morning. What is the best definition of the word labor in this sentence?
B.why: “Before the baby was born” selects the childbirth sense of labor.

whyNot.0: Physical work is the everyday sense of labor; the baby's birth rules it out here.
whyNot.2: Paid workers (a labor force) is another sense the sentence rules out.
whyNot.3: A hospital stay is a topic fit, but labor here is the process of birth itself.

C.q: The manager tried to mollify the angry visitor by offering a quiet room and a cup of coffee. Based on the context, what does mollify mean?
C.why: General sense: the visitor is angry, and a quiet room and coffee are meant to calm him. Mollify means to soothe.

whyNot.0: Enraging is the opposite of the manager's goal.
whyNot.1: Notify is a look-alike ending (-ify) meaning to inform.
whyNot.2: Offering coffee does not question anyone; it is meant to calm.

C.q: The nurse sent a throat culture to the lab to check for strep bacteria. What is the best definition of the word culture in this sentence?
C.why: “Sent to the lab” and “check for bacteria” select the lab sense: a sample grown to detect microorganisms.

whyNot.0: Customs and beliefs is the everyday sense; the lab and bacteria rule it out.
whyNot.2: Arts and interests is another everyday sense that does not fit a lab test.
whyNot.3: Strep is an infection, a topic fit, but the culture is the sample, not the illness.

C.q: “Many of the hospital's longtime volunteers are octogenarians; in other words, they are in their eighties.” Which type of context clue helps the reader understand octogenarians?
C.why: “In other words” is a definition/restatement signal: the sentence directly restates the term as people in their eighties.

whyNot.0: There is no contrast word such as “but” or “unlike,” and no opposite is described.
whyNot.1: No list introduced by “such as” or “including” appears.
whyNot.2: No “because” or “therefore” links a cause to a result.

reteach.title: Fill in the smudged word
reteach.question: A coffee spill has smudged one word on a note from your roommate: “I'm ______ tonight, so please don't wake me before 6 a.m.” You know what the word must be without seeing it. That instinct is context-clue reading.

blocks.body: You filled the smudge with “exhausted” or “working late” because the rest of the note left only a few possibilities. An unfamiliar word on the HESI A2 is just a smudge you can see: “I'm somnolent tonight, so please don't wake me.” Treat it as blank, use the surrounding words to predict, and then pick the option that fits the gap. Somnolent means sleepy.

steps.label: Match an option
steps.sub: the one that fits the gap

blocks.text: Do not let a word's look decide. “Somnolent” looks like “solemn,” but substitution shows only “sleepy” fits the note.

explain.body: A definition clue states the meaning, often after “or,” “that is” or “in other words.” A synonym clue places a word with a similar meaning nearby, often signaled by “also,” “likewise” or “and.”

test.q: The guide called the cave labyrinthine; likewise, the tunnels beneath the old hospital formed a maze of twisting passages. Based on the context, what does labyrinthine mean?
test.why: “Likewise” signals a synonym clue: the tunnels are similarly “a maze of twisting passages.” Labyrinthine means complex and winding.

whyNot.0: Caves are often dark and damp, a topic fit, but the clue describes a maze.
whyNot.1: “Old hospital” describes the building's age, not the meaning of the target word.
whyNot.3: The clue describes twisting, not narrowness or slope.

explain.body: A contrast clue sets the unknown word against its opposite, signaled by “but,” “however,” “unlike,” “whereas” or “instead.” Find the opposite, then flip it.

steps.label: Read the other side
steps.sub: said it in half the words

test.q: Whereas the first draft of the safety report was verbose, the final version said the same thing in half the words. Based on the context, what does verbose mean?
test.why: “Whereas” sets up a contrast with a version that said the same thing in half the words, so the first draft was wordy.

whyNot.0: This describes the final version, the opposite side of the contrast.
whyNot.1: The contrast is about length, not accuracy.
whyNot.2: Wordy writing can be hard to follow, but the clue contrasts the number of words.

explain.body: Example clues list instances after “such as,” “including” or “for example”: ask what the items have in common. Cause-and-effect clues (“because,” “so,” “as a result”) reveal the meaning through what caused something or what it led to.

test.q: Ella collects ephemera, including ticket stubs, postcards and newspaper clippings that most people throw away within days. Based on the context, what are ephemera?
test.why: The examples share two features: they are printed paper and people discard them quickly. Ephemera are printed items not meant to last.

whyNot.0: Furniture is not printed and does not match tickets or clippings.
whyNot.2: Coins are metal and are not thrown away within days.
whyNot.3: Letters from famous people are kept, not thrown away within days.

explain.body: Many common words have two or more senses. Read the rest of the sentence for the word that decides: a bruise decides tender (sore), an amount decides minute (tiny), a lab test decides culture (a grown sample).

test.q: The surgeon warned the family that the patient's injuries were grave and needed surgery that night. What is the best definition of the word grave in this sentence?
test.why: Grave describes the injuries (an adjective), and the need for surgery that night shows they were very serious.

whyNot.0: A burial place is the noun sense; here grave describes injuries.
whyNot.2: Healing speed is a topic fit, but grave means serious, not slow.
whyNot.3: Nothing in the sentence says the injuries were hidden; grave means serious.
